name: Content Placeholder 2
text: In 1995, a US Army Blackhawk battalion reported 89% readiness. But when ordered to deploy, the commander mandated that no aircraft could deploy if it had less than 75 hours remaining until its next phase maintenance (Pippin, 1998).9 of 24 helicopters were immediately non-deployable due to poor maintenance staggering.This represented a massive loss of power.

name: TextBox 4
text: Priority VNS delivered a practical baseline

name: TextBox 12
text: What works well and what is still limited

name: TextBox 13
text: • We focus first on maintenance that hits the worst availability days.• When we move a check, we rebuild that aircraft’s later schedule so rules stay valid.• We update availability cheaply instead of recalculating from scratch.• Currently we only accept better moves and we stop when nothing improves.

name: TextBox 9
text: Same priority-based selection neighbour search algorithm

name: TextBox 11
text: Better moves are always kept. Worse moves can still be kept early on, by chance.

name: TextBox 13
text: Over time we accept fewer worse moves, so the search settles on a strong plan.

name: TextBox 16
text: Think of the search like walking over hills. Today’s method only walks uphill. That is fast and safe, but you can get stuck on a steep part of the hill when a better peak is nearby.Simulated annealing sometimes takes a downhill step early, so you can leave a trap and reach a better overall schedule. As the search “cools,” those downhill steps become rare, and we settle on the best plan we found.

name: TextBox 4
text: How annealing fits into our design

name: TextBox 7
text: • Focus on the worst availability days firstRebuild the aircraft schedule after each moveUpdate availability without recalculating everythingTry larger timing shifts, then smaller ones

name: TextBox 10
text: Currently: only keep the improving movesNew method: annealing accept better moves always, worse moves sometimes, depending how early and lateDrop best improvement strategy so worse candidates can be tried

name: TextBox 12
text: Verdict: Keep how we find candidate moves. Change how we decide which moves to accept.

name: TextBox 28
text: If the new schedule improves worst-day availability, keep it. That always comes first.

name: TextBox 30
text: If it lowers the minimum availability, reject it. Do not accept a “smoother” plan that makes the busiest day worse.

name: TextBox 32
text: If the worst day is unchanged, but the plan is bumpier or lower on average, allow it sometimes early, less often as the search cools.

name: TextBox 33
text: What we report, and how we test

name: TextBox 34
text: Because annealing is random, run the full search 3 times and report the typical result. Current priority selection NS method needs one run, do not compare the best of three with one baseline run.

name: TextBox 4
text: Basin-hopping did not clear the keep rule

name: TextBox 12
text: Same heavy forecast. Lower spread is the smoother plan.

name: TextBox 13
text: • Tuned hill-climb, one run: spread 1.392, about 116 seconds.• Basin-hopping, median of seeds 1–3: spread 1.390, about 306 seconds. Two seeds ran past five minutes.• Tightened acceptance, which keeps the worst day from falling, matched the hill-climb at 1.392.• The keep rule asked for a 0.005 smoother plan, worst day still 18, and a typical run within five minutes.

name: TextBox 4
text: Separate start effect from algorithm gain

name: TextBox 14
text: The search only makes local moves from the original plan.A well-staggered start can look like a better algorithm.A bunched start can make a good method look weaker.

name: TextBox 18
text: Build a few controlled starts: bunched, as-loaded, and more spread out.Run current method and annealing from each of those same starts.Document how much the initial stagger impacts the optimisation.

name: TextBox 6
text: Priority targeting does not cancel this.

name: TextBox 7
text: It only chooses which events to try first. Days that are not the current worst days keep the original stagger, so a good start can still do some of the work.

name: TextBox 4
text: The as-loaded opening still finishes smoothest

name: TextBox 12
text: Every opening starts at a worst day of 15 and finishes at 18

name: TextBox 13
text: • Spread opening: finished spread 1.417, in 93 seconds.• Figures are the tuned hill-climb. Basin-hopping was about 0.001 to 0.003 smoother on each opening, and slower.• Bunching or spreading the first checks leaves a bumpier finished plan.• The as-loaded forecast remains the start we keep.

name: TextBox 4
text: What we will keep, and when we stop

name: TextBox 7
text: Worst-day availability must be as good as current algorithm.Runtime does not increase too much.New operational rules still produce legal, usable schedules.The gain is from the method, not a luckier start or a luckier seed.

name: TextBox 10
text: Annealing does not beat the current method, and we  will keep the current method.Worse moves start hurting the minimum availability,  we tighten the acceptance rule.New constraints break feasibility.

name: TextBox 4
text: The tuned hill-climb is the method we take forward

name: TextBox 13
text: • Priority search, rebuild after each move, and accept an improving plan only.• Half-step shifts are passed in. The published Iteration 1 defaults stay as they were.• The spread gain was 0.001, short of 0.005, and the typical run passed five minutes.• Tightened acceptance found the same plan as the hill-climb.
